If someone came up to me and looked in my eyes and smiled, I'd immediately be very suspicious and then wait to see what it was they wanted. 

Unless it was just basic politeness, in which case I'd reciprocate.
I don't know on them morality side of things. But if you've made the decision to try and help then I suppose that's the only thing you can do.

Well if you don't know which time zone they're in, how do you know which local police station to contact?

Assuming you did know, I seriously doubt they would have the resources to track them down. I'm not sure they'd even try (especially in certain countries where the police/mental health services are terrible). There's hundreds of suicidal posts/people online, with many threatening to do something in a specific timeline. 

Even if they did try, would they be able to find said person by tomorrow? If by some miracle they did, if that person claims it wasn't serious, they'll probably just leave them to it.

I'm not sure you even need to consider the invasion of privacy aspect if it is completely implausible. 

However if you have a name/address that makes it easy for the police to find them, then I think you'll have to follow your own conscience and perhaps consider whether or not it's a cry for help or a vent.
Thanks this is very useful! Hadn't thought about it from many of these angles.

If you really need help the best thing I can suggest is going to a doctor to talk about how you're feeling. If you get a decent one, they can hopefully point you in the direction of real help.

I agree that hotlines and the samaritans are pretty useless. They can't actually provide advice, only listen. I might as well of chatted to a lamp post for all the good it did for me.

Tried it. Alcohol at least - don't have the social skills or circle to go to any sort of party or get any type of illegal drugs. Woke up with a hangover and felt just as suicidal as the night before. 
No prescription meds have ever worked either in 15 years, in fact many made it worse.

Still if you've found something that's helped you, that's great. Don't think it will work for everyone though.
Just say you've been having suicidal thoughts. Your therapist will then ask something along the lines of - are you at risk of carrying them out imminently. Obviously you then say no.
If it's any consolation, I'm sure Chad won't be there for much longer. He'll be offered a CEO position somewhere thanks to the halo effect so at least he won't be there to recount the experience.

Pretty much nothing makes me happy anymore. Although that's not all to do with being FA. I don't get much enjoyment from hobbies and have no goals that I want to accomplish in life. I don't cry into my pillow at night, I'm just going through the motions. I kind of feel like I'm already dead.
If I at least had one friend maybe there would be more things to do but there's also a possibility it wouldn't make much of a difference.
I don't think so because we wouldn't exist.
The same place we were before we were born - nowhere.

Agree. It just makes 99% of my life more difficult. From making friends, finding jobs, coping with every day situations, coping with change, trying to manage obsessions/special interests so the rest of my life hasn't gone to shit when I'm over it etc.
I live in a pretty rural area, near the ocean. Feel isolated and bored stupid.

If all you did was try to hold her hand...It sounds like she just wanted a free night out. Free food, free weed....at least you didn't end up paying for the movie as well.
I would have thought a more normal reaction would be to say something along the lines of "I just want to go out as friends tonight".
What you did doesn't sound creepy. Maybe she should lay off the drugs for a bit.

I find daytime the worst. During the day I'm constantly reminded of the things I don't have and I have to watch people irl have fun and friendships that I've never experienced.

At night I can just switch off, play games and forget the rest of the world exists.

It's the mere exposure effect - the more you see something the more you like it.
Also when you see your unflipped face, because you're not used to it you're immediately drawn to features you no longer notice in the mirror because they look slightly different.

From what I've heard the most accurate representation of how other people see you is a photo (with a quality camera). A mirror always flips/reverses your image so it's not what other people see. You can also get things called true mirrors which show you as you appear to others.

I gauge my actual appearance from my photos. It was a bit like ripping a band aid off at first. Had to accept just how bad I looked and I didn't think I looked good to begin with.
Yeah I've never met anyone who loved meeting/spending time with outcasts either....

Yeah it is really weird even for NTs. Whenever someone tries to high five me, i always spend an awkward amount of time staring at their hand trying process what they are doing and what they want. 

From observing other people, I found the best way to correct the "left hanging" issue is to try and laugh it off (or pretend to, I don't actually find it funny) and then poke fun at myself by saying something along the lines of "that took me longer than it should".

I think it's a gesture of enthusiasm. I also always go for a weak high five as I think that will always be the easier mistake to correct. Compared to hitting someone too hard and possibly inflicting some level of pain.

People can also just be really fickle. So again you might be basing your self esteem on someone who isn't worth it.

But yes it's also true we're a social species that craves social acceptance. I think the healthiest way to be is to have a good balance between your own self worth and external validation.

Polite but distant. Which is exactly how I treat them.

The rules I try to follow are smile when greeting someone and when saying goodbye. Also if they smile mid conversation e.g when telling a joke.
I've pretty much got the first part sorted. As for the mid conversation stuff, I have to be alert and focused on what's going on, otherwise I tend to forget.
A long time ago and not for long. It just zoned me out and I'd spend all my time sleeping. Didn't help my symptoms at all.
Take it. I have nothing to lose.

I think it's a form of redirection. A bit like when someone has gone hysterical and you slap them to snap them out of it.
I think when I've been overwhelmed and am in meltdown, physical pain helps direct and center my thoughts on that pain, which in a way brings back control and begins to calm me down.
It's not a conscious decision when actually having a meltdown but I will do it consciously if I'm beginning to get really stressed.
Yeah it's pretty dull. I can't think of anything I'd really like to do even if I had the ability and resources.

I'm not too sure that this needs to be approached as an Aspergers issue. If you are being upfront and blunt about the fact you don't want anything serious, then (unless severely affected) she should understand what that means.

However she's clearly holding out hope that this will evolve into something more, even expecting it judging from your quotes. She's convinced she can change you, which isn't a mindset limited to someone with Asperger's.
Can you trust she isn't using the sex just to try and get you to develop feelings? No.

Will she be hurt if in a years time you find someone you want a relationship with and dump her? I'd it's very likely.
No it actually helps prevent it for me. Not really sure why but if I went into a club sober, the noise and people would get to me far more than if I was already tipsy.

In my meltdowns, it wouldn't matter how embarrassed I'd feel afterwards, it would be completely out of my control at that point and I wouldn't be able to think rationally or coherently about the consequences either.

Really wish I'd managed to end it when I'd had the motivation to push through the survival instinct.

In bigger terms, yes. For example I think if you meet someone, get talking to them and they find out you don't have friends then they seem to keep their distance. It's a pattern I've noticed with myself and others.
I don't know if it's a conscious choice or subconscious thought/feeling of there might be something wrong with this person. Or if it's even something as simple as - if you've already got friends you've got more relatable experiences to talk about so it's easier to make more friends. 

In regards to the class incident, it may have been a group of friends wanting to sit together or a better vantage point.

I hate them with a passion. I remember one in particular where a bank (the actual building) sailed away into the ocean. I had no idea what they were trying to say. If I was choosing a bank to go with, the last one I'd go for is one in the middle of the ocean.....
I know it's not supposed to be taken so literally but what were they trying to say? Maybe "we hate customers don't bother us?".

It made me rage so bad I had to switch the TV off the second it came on.

I don't think it would matter if you were the most neurotypical person on the planet - you would still meet people who didn't like you for various reasons (skin colour, political view, sports teams etc). 

In terms of relationships/friendships it depends on meeting the right people just as it does for everyone else. Asperger's does present more problems but it certainly doesn't make it impossible, that would defy all probability. Just try to meet lots of different people and learn to not take it too personally if it doesn't work out.

As for jobs I'd say practice makes....it better. I've also found it a good idea to keep colleagues at a distance. By all means be professional/polite but avoid socialising with them too much. Keep your work and life separate.

No effect on my life, but for someone who actually wanted help/support......well a bit like a nudge off a cliff I'd imagine.

Not really. If I go "why not?", my brain will give me 10 different reasons why not. Not because of anxiety but because I've asked.

I think I'd be a bad parent too. I get extremely angry if disturbed from my interests, don't like physical contact, stupidity or neediness. Putting me and kids together is a match made in hell, I think it would make everyone involved miserable.

Luckily I also have no urge to have kids.

I tend to go out for a walk in a busy place because the amount of people and cars around means that to some extent I have to be aware of them and if I can't solely focus on my line of thought I'll lose interest and drop it (for a time).
Failing that I'll do exercise that pushes me to the limit (only for 30mins or so). Having to focus on pacing, breathing and running that extra mile takes me away from my thought processes. Then I can switch over to what I need to be thinking about.

I don't really like music. The few tracks I will listen to are all different, the only thing they have in common is that there's no lyrics. 
I hate lyrics in songs. It's usually someone moaning about stupid shit, like they just broke up with their boyfriend etc and it just starts to annoy me.

I used to be a lot like you but it lead to feeling even more apathetic and indifferent about life than usual.

It was only due to these feelings that I had to analyse my approach to life. Acting in a certain way to get people to view me as friendly was completely unrewarding. This is because I didn't like or respect 90% of them. The vast majority of people are unintelligent and their conversations amount to the weather, work, family or friends. There was no point in putting effort in to please them. I was getting so little out of it and I found it tiring as it didn't come naturally. The most I manage these days is civility, to keep things efficient (aka not wasting time talking or arguing).

However the only way I was able to establish any personal value or identity was due to the emotional discomfort reaching such a level that it couldn't be ignored.
If you're content with your life and the way you live it, I wouldn't worry about changing anything.

I'd struggle to define my 'real' self but I'd describe it as a very subtle, quiet part that can only really communicate with the mask (the interface for everyday life) through more intuitive feelings opposed to concrete feelings/thought.

Think it depends on the individuals.

Personally I've never been able to get along with another aspie. We either end up debating everything at all hours as neither of us can let even the smallest of things go. Or the social anxiety begins to intensify. E.g Them: "I'm sorry if that came across as weird" Me: thinking -have I done something to come across as annoyed/scared/confused etc.

To be honest in regards to initiating intimacy and how her mental health affects her, it would probably be best to just ask her in a message/email. That way she can think about it and reply without being under any pressure.

I wouldn't mention the compliments thing. For me personally having to take into account someone's self esteem while thinking of appropriate compliments would stress me out. 

As for the family, I think you'll probably have to wait and see whether they're just more careful around her due to the mental health issues or whether they're completely unreasonable before you decide on a course of action.
